entries.26edd0989552a7a97e6df4007db3e532052f54fc: <div sID="gen3663" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Deut.18" sID="Deut.18"/> <div eID="gen3663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3664" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3665" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The rights and revenues of the church are settled, and rules given concerning the Levites' ministration and maintenance, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1-Deut.18.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. The caution against the idolatrous abominable customs of the heathen is repeated, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.9-Deut.18.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. III. A promise is given them of the spirit of prophecy to continue among them, and to centre at last in Christ the great prophet, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15-Deut.18.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. IV. Wrath threatened against those that despise prophecy (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.19">ver. 19</reference>) or counterfeit it (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">ver. 20</reference>), and a rule given for the trial of it, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.21-Deut.18.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>.
entries.047ed0486f52c20e20b5dccd2dc869d5b64efd47: <div eID="gen3665" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3664" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Maintenance of the Levites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The priests the Levites, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel: they shall eat the offerings of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made by fire, and his inheritance. <hi type="super">2</hi> Therefore shall they have no inheritance among their brethren: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> their inheritance, as he hath said unto them. <hi type="super">3</hi> And this shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> ox or sheep; and they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. <hi type="super">4</hi> The firstfruits <hi type="italic">also</hi> of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep, shalt thou give him. <hi type="super">5</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath chosen him out of all thy tribes, to stand to minister in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , him and his sons for ever. <hi type="super">6</hi> And if a Levite come from any of thy gates out of all Israel, where he sojourned, and come with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall choose; <hi type="super">7</hi> Then he shall minister in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God, as all his brethren the Levites <hi type="italic">do,</hi> which stand there before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> They shall have like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony. <div eID="gen3666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3667" type="x-p"/> Magistracy and ministry are two divine institutions of admirable use for the support and advancement of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God among men.</hi> Laws concerning the former we had in the close of the foregoing chapter, directions are in this given concerning the latter. Land-marks are here set between the estates of the priests and those of the people. <div eID="gen3667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3668" type="x-p"/> I. Care is taken that the priests entangle not themselves with the affairs of this life, nor enrich themselves with the wealth of this world; they have better things to mind. They <hi type="italic">shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel,</hi> that is, no share either in the spoils taken in war or in the land that was to be divided by lot, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">v. 1</reference>. Their warfare and husbandry are both spiritual, and enough to fill their hands both with work and profit and to content them. <hi type="italic">The Lord is their inheritance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.18.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, Those that have God for their inheritance, according to the new covenant, should not be greedy of great things in the world, neither gripe what they have nor grasp at more, but look upon all present things with the indifference which becomes those that believe God to be all-sufficient. <div eID="gen3668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3669" type="x-p"/> II. Care is likewise taken that they want not any of the comforts and conveniences of this life. Though God, who is a Spirit, is their inheritance, it does not therefore follow that they must live upon the air; no, <div eID="gen3669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3670" type="x-p"/> 1. The people must provide for them. They must have their <hi type="italic">due from the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.18.3">v. 3</reference>. Their maintenance must not depend upon the generosity of the people, but they must be by law entitled to it. He that is taught in the word ought in justice to communicate to him that teaches him; and he that has the benefit of solemn religious assemblies ought to contribute to the comfortable support of those that preside in such assemblies. (1.) The priests who in their courses served at the altar had their share of the sacrifices, namely, the peace-offerings, that were brought while they were in waiting: besides the breast and shoulder, which were appointed them before (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.32-Lev.7.34">Lev. vii. 32-34</reference>), the cheeks and maw are here ordered to be given them; so far was the law from diminishing what was already granted that it gave them an augmentation (2.) The first-fruits which arose within such a precinct were brought in, as it should seem, to the priests that resided among them, for their maintenance in the country; the first of their corn and wine for food, and the first of their fleece for clothing (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.4">v. 4</reference>); for the priests who were employed to teach others ought themselves to learn, having food and raiment, to be therewith content. The first-fruits were devoted to God, and he constituted the priests his receivers; and if God reckons what is, in general, given to the poor, lent to him, to be repaid with interest, much more what is, in particular, given to the poor, lent to him, to be repaid with interest, much more what is, in particular, given to poor ministers. There is a good reason given for this constant charge upon their estates (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.5">v. 5</reference>), because the Levites were <hi type="italic">chosen of God,</hi> and his choice must be owned and countenanced, and those honoured by us whom he honours; and <hi type="italic">because they stood to minister,</hi> and ought to be recompensed for their attendance and labour, especially since it was <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord,</hi> by his warrant, in his service, and for his praise, and this charge entailed upon their seed for ever; those who were thus engaged and thus employed ought to have all due encouragement given them, as some of the most needful useful members of their commonwealth. <div eID="gen3670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3671" type="x-p"/> 2. The priests must not themselves stand in one another's light. If a priest that by the law was obliged to serve at the altar only in his turn, and was paid for that, should, out of his great affection to the sanctuary, devote himself to a constant attendance there, and quit the ease and pleasure of the city in which he had his lot for the satisfaction of serving the altar, the priests whose turn it was to attend must admit him both to join in the work and to share in the wages, and not grudge him either the honour of the one or the profit of the other, though it might seem to break in upon them, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.6-Deut.18.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Note, A hearty pious zeal to serve God and his church, though it may a little encroach upon a settled order, and there may be somewhat in it that looks irregular, yet ought to be gratified and not discouraged. He that appears to have a hearty affection to the sanctuary, and loves dearly to be employed in the service of it, <hi type="italic">in God's name let him minister;</hi> he shall be as welcome to God as the Levites whose course it was to minister, and should be so to them. The settling of the courses was intended rather to secure those to the work that were not willing to do so much than to exclude any that were willing to do more. And he that thus serves as a volunteer shall have as good pay as the pressed men, <hi type="italic">besides that which comes of the sale of his patrimony.</hi> The church of Rome obliges those who leave their estates to go into a monastery to bring the produce of their estates with them into the common stock of the monastery, for gain is their godliness; but here it is ordered that the pious devotee should reserve to himself the produce of his patrimony, for religion and the ministry were never appointed of God, however they have been abused by men, to serve a secular interest.
entries.847e5e0082bf749eb7a37d407a683de94eeec873: <div eID="gen3671" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Idolatrous Customs of the Canaanites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> When thou art come into the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations. <hi type="super">10</hi> There shall not be found among you <hi type="italic">any one</hi> that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, <hi type="italic">or</hi> that useth divination, <hi type="italic">or</hi> an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, <hi type="super">11</hi> Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. <hi type="super">12</hi> For all that do these things <hi type="italic">are</hi> an abomination unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and because of these abominations the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God doth drive them out from before thee. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt be perfect with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. <hi type="super">14</hi> For these nations, which thou shalt possess, hearkened unto observers of times, and unto diviners: but as for thee, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath not suffered thee so <hi type="italic">to do.</hi> <div eID="gen3672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3673" type="x-p"/> One would not think there had been so much need as it seems there was to arm the people of Israel against the infection of the idolatrous customs of the Canaanites. Was it possible that a people so blessed with divine institutions should ever admit the brutish and barbarous inventions of men and devils? Were they in any danger of making those their tutors and directors in religion whom God had made their captives and tributaries? It seems they were in danger, and therefore, after many similar cautions, they are here charged not to do after the abominations of those nations, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.9">v. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen3673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3674" type="x-p"/> I. Some particulars are specified; as, 1. The consecrating of their children to Moloch, an idol that represented the sun, by making them to <hi type="italic">pass through the fire,</hi> and sometimes consuming them as sacrifices in the fire, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">v. 10</reference>. See the law against this before, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev. xviii. 21</reference>. 2. Using arts of divination, to get the unnecessary knowledge of things to come, <hi type="italic">enchantments, witchcrafts, charms, &c.,</hi> by which the power and knowledge peculiar to God were attributed to the devil, to the great reproach both of God's counsels and of his providence, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10-Deut.18.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. One would wonder that such arts and works of darkness, so senseless and absurd, so impious and profane, could be found in a country where divine revelation shone so clearly; yet we find remains of them even where Christ's holy religion is known and professed; such are the powers and policies of the <hi type="italic">rulers of the darkness of this world.</hi> But let those give heed to fortune-tellers, or go to wizards for the discovery of things secret, that use spells for the cure of diseases, are in any league or acquaintance with familiar spirits, or form a confederacy with those that are—let them know that they can have no fellowship with God while thus they have fellowship with devils. It is amazing to think that there should by any pretenders of this kind in such a land and day of light as we live in. <div eID="gen3674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3675" type="x-p"/> II. Some reasons are given against their conformity to the customs of the Gentiles. 1. Because it would make them abominable to God. The things themselves being hateful to him, those that do them are an abomination; and miserable is that creature that has become odious to its Creator, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.12">v. 12</reference>. See the malignity and mischievousness of sin; that must needs be an evil thing indeed which provokes the God of mercy to detest the work of his own hands. 2. Because these abominable practices had been the ruin of the Canaanites, of which ruin they were not only the witnesses but the instruments. It would be the most inexcusable folly, as well as the most unpardonable impiety, for them to practise themselves those very things for which they had been employed so severely to chastise others. Did the land spue out the abominations of the Canaanites, and shall Israel lick up the vomit? 3. Because they were <hi type="italic">better taught,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.18.13-Deut.18.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. It is an argument like that of the apostle against Christians walking as the Gentiles walked (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.17-Eph.4.18">Eph. iv. 17, 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.20">20</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have not so learned Christ.</hi> "It is true these nations, whom God <hi type="italic">gave up to their own hearts' lusts, and suffered to walk in their own ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.16">Acts xiv. 16</reference>), did thus corrupt themselves; but thou art not thus abandoned by the grace of God: <hi type="italic">the Lord thy God had not suffered thee to do so;</hi> thou art instructed in divine things, and hast fair warning given thee of the evil of those practices; and therefore, whatever others do, it is expected that thou shouldest be <hi type="italic">perfect with the Lord thy God,</hi>" that is, "that thou shouldest give divine honours to him, to him only, and to no other, and not mix any of the superstitious customs of the heathen with his institutions." One of the Chaldee paraphrasts here takes notice of God's furnishing them with the oracle of urim and thummim, as a preservative from all unlawful arts of divination. Those were fools indeed who would go to consult the father of lies when they had such a ready way of consulting the God of truth.
entries.0a628ccb5e4a2a1cc4934fbfcd2f45892ed610e4: <div eID="gen3675" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Great Prophet; False Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken; <hi type="super">16</hi> According to all that thou desiredst of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, Let me not hear again the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, They have well <hi type="italic">spoken that</hi> which they have spoken. <hi type="super">18</hi> I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him. <hi type="super">19</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require <hi type="italic">it</hi> of him. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die. <hi type="super">21</hi> And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not spoken? <hi type="super">22</hi> When a prophet speaketh in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> the thing which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not spoken, <hi type="italic">but</hi> the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him. <div eID="gen3676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3677" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The promise of the great prophet, with a command to receive him, and hearken to him. Now, <div eID="gen3677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3678" type="x-p"/> 1. Some think it is the promise of a succession of prophets, that should for many ages be kept up in Israel. Besides the priests and Levites, their ordinary ministers, whose office it was to teach Jacob God's law, they should have prophets, extraordinary ministers, to reprove them for their faults, remind them of their duty, and foretel things to come, judgments for warning and deliverances for their comfort. Having these prophets, (1.) They need not use divinations, nor consult with familiar spirits, for they might enquire of God's prophets even concerning their private affairs, as Saul did when he was in quest of his father's asses, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1 Sam. ix. 6</reference>. (2.) They could not miss the way of their duty through ignorance or mistake, nor differ in their opinions about it, having prophets among them, whom, in every difficult doubtful case, they might advise with and appeal to. These prophets were like unto Moses in some respects, though far inferior to him, <reference osisRef="Deut.34.10">Deut. xxxiv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen3678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3679" type="x-p"/> 2. Whether a succession of prophets be included in this promise or not, we are sure that it is primarily intended as a promise of Christ, and it is the clearest promise of him that is in all the law of Moses. It is expressly applied to our Lord Jesus as the Messiah promised (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.22">Acts iii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.37">vii. 37</reference>), and the people had an eye to this promise when they said concerning him, <hi type="italic">This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.14">John vi. 14</reference>); and it was his Spirit that spoke in all the other prophets, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen3679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3680" type="x-p"/> (1.) What it is that is here promised concerning Christ. What God promised Moses at Mount Sinai (which he relates, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">v. 18</reference>), he promised the people (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">v. 15</reference>) in God's name. [1.] That there should come a prophet, great above all the prophets, by whom God would make known himself and his will to the children of men more fully and clearly than ever he had done before. He is the <hi type="italic">light of the world,</hi> as prophecy was of the Jewish church, <reference osisRef="John.8.12">John viii. 12</reference>. He is the Word, by whom God speaks to us, <reference osisRef="John.1.1">John i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">Heb. i. 2</reference>. [2.] That God would <hi type="italic">raise him up from the midst of them.</hi> In his birth he should be one of that nation, should live among them and be sent to them. In his resurrection he should be <hi type="italic">raised up at Jerusalem,</hi> and thence his doctrine should go forth to all the world: thus God, having raised up his Son Christ Jesus, sent him to bless us. [3.] That he should be like unto Moses, only as much above him as the other prophets came short of him. Moses was such a prophet as was a law-giver to Israel and their deliverer out of Egypt, and so was Christ: he not only teaches, but rules and saves. Moses was the founder of a new dispensation by signs and wonders and mighty deeds, and so was Christ, by which he proved himself a teacher come from God. Was Moses faithful? So was Christ; Moses as a servant, but Christ as a Son. [4.] That God would put his words in his mouth, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">v. 18</reference>. What messages God had to send to the children of men he would send them by him, and give him full instructions what to say and do as a prophet. Hence our Saviour says, <hi type="italic">My doctrine is not mine</hi> originally, <hi type="italic">but his that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.16">John vii. 16</reference>. So that this great promise is performed; this Prophet has come, even Jesus; it is he that should come, and we are to look for no other. <div eID="gen3680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3681" type="x-p"/> (2.) The agreeableness of this designed dispensation to the people's avowed choice and desire at Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.16-Deut.18.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. There God had spoken to them in thunder and lightning, out of the midst of the fire and thick darkness. Every word made their ears tingle and their hearts tremble, so that the whole congregation was ready to die with fear. In this fright, they begged hard that God would not speak to them in this manner any more (they could not bear it, it would overwhelm and distract them), but that he would speak to them by men like themselves, by Moses now, and afterwards by other prophets like unto him. "Well," says God, "it shall be so; they shall be spoken to by men, whose <hi type="italic">terrors shall not make them afraid;</hi>" and, to crown the favour beyond what they were able to ask or think, in the fulness of time the Word itself was made flesh, and they saw his glory as of the <hi type="italic">only-begotten of the Father,</hi> not, as at Mount Sinai, full of majesty and terror, <hi type="italic">but full of grace and truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>. Thus, in answer to the request of those who were struck with amazement by the law, God promised the incarnation of his Son, though we may suppose it far from the thoughts of those that made that request. <div eID="gen3681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3682" type="x-p"/> (3.) A charge and command given to all people to hear and believe, hear and obey, this great prophet here promised: <hi type="italic">Unto him you shall hearken</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">v. 15</reference>); and whoever will not hearken to him shall be surely and severely reckoned with for his contempt (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will require it of him.</hi> God himself applied this to our Lord Jesus in the <hi type="italic">voice that came out of the excellent glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Matt. xvii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Hear you him,</hi> that is, this is he concerning whom it was said by Moses of old, <hi type="italic">Unto him you shall hearken;</hi> and Moses and Elias then stood by and assented to it. The sentence here passed on those that hearken not to this prophet is repeated and ratified in the New Testament. <hi type="italic">He that believeth not the Son, the wrath of God abideth on him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">And how shall we escape if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven?</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.25">Heb. xii. 25</reference>. The Chaldee paraphrase here reads it, <hi type="italic">My Word shall require it of him,</hi> which can be no other than a divine person, Christ the eternal Word, to whom the Father has committed all judgement, and by whom he will at the last day judge the world. Whoever turns a deaf ear to Jesus Christ shall find that it is at his peril; the same that is the prophet is to be his judge, <reference osisRef="John.12.48">John xii. 48</reference>. <div eID="gen3682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3683" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a caution against false prophets, 1. By way of threatening against the pretenders themselves, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">v. 20</reference>. Whoever sets up for a prophet, and produces either a commission from the true God, shall be deemed and adjudged guilty of high treason against the crown and dignity of the King of kings, and that traitor shall be put to death (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">v. 20</reference>), namely, by the judgment of the great sanhedrim, which, in process of time, sat at Jerusalem; and therefore our Saviour says that a prophet could not perish but at Jerusalem, and lays the blood of the prophets at Jerusalem's door (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.33-Luke.13.34">Luke xiii. 33, 34</reference>), whom therefore God himself would punish; yet <hi type="italic">there</hi> false prophets were supported. 2. By way of direction to the people, that they might not be imposed upon by pretenders, of which there were many, as appears, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.25">Jer. xxiii. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.6">Ezek. xiii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.6">1 Kings xxii. 6</reference>. It is a very proper question which they are supposed to ask, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.21">v. 21</reference>. Since it is so great a duty to hearken to the true prophets, and yet there is so much danger of being misled by false prophets, <hi type="italic">how shall we know the word which the Lord has not spoken?</hi> By what marks may we discover a cheat? Note, It highly concerns us to have a right touchstone wherewith to try the word we hear, that we may know what that word is which the Lord has not spoken. Whatever is directly repugnant to sense, to the light and law of nature, and to the plain meaning of the written word, we may be sure is not that which the Lord has spoken; nor that which gives countenance and encouragement to sin, or has a manifest tendency to the destruction of piety or charity: far be it from God that he should contradict himself. The rule here given in answer to this enquiry was adapted chiefly to that state, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.22">v. 22</reference>. If there was any cause to suspect the sincerity of a prophet, let them observe that if he gave them any sign, or foretold something to come, and the event was not according to his prediction, they might be sure he was not sent of God. This does not refer so much to the foretelling of mercies and judgments (though as to these, and the difference between the predictions of mercies and judgments, there is a rule of discerning between truth and falsehood laid down by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.8-Jer.28.9">Jer. xxviii. 8, 9</reference>), but rather to the giving of signs on purpose to confirm their mission. Though the sign did come to pass, yet this would not serve to prove their mission if they called them to serve other gods; this point had been already settled, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.3">Deut. xiii. 1-3</reference>. But, if the sign did not come to pass, this would serve to disprove their mission. "When Moses cast his rod upon the ground (it is bishop Patrick's explanation of this), and said it would become a serpent, if it had not accordingly been turned into a serpent, Moses had been a false prophet: if, when Elijah called for fire from heaven to consume the sacrifice, none had come, he had been no better than the prophets of Baal." Samuel's mission was proved by this, that <hi type="italic">God let none of his words fall to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.19-1Sam.3.20">1 Sam. iii. 19, 20</reference>. And by the miracles Christ wrought, especially by that great sign he gave of his resurrection the third day, which came to pass as he foretold, it appeared that he was a teacher come from God. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> They are directed not to be afraid of a false prophet; that is, not to be afraid of the judgments such a one might denounce to amuse people and strike terror upon them; nor to be afraid of executing the law upon him when, upon a strict and impartial scrutiny, it appeared that he was a false prophet. This command not to fear a false prophet implies that a true prophet, who proved his commission by clear and undeniable proofs, was to be feared, and it was at their peril if they offered him any violence or put any slight upon him.  <chapter eID="Deut.18"/> <div eID="gen3683" type="x-p"/>

entries.d108db6c232f064822eeeb68124d11443ae14b64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1815"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.18.1-Deut.18.8">De 18:1-8</reference>. The Lord Is the Priests' and the Levites' Inheritance.</title> <div sID="gen2428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1815"/><hi type="bold">1. The priests the Levites ... shall eat the offerings--</hi>As the tribe of Levi had no inheritance allotted them like the other tribes but were wholly consecrated to the priestly office, their maintenance was to arise from tithes, first-fruits, and certain portions of the oblations presented on the altar, which God having by express appointment reserved to Himself made over, after being offered, to His ministers. <div eID="gen2428" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d63335b39589d031c911525a63c4b87d6f3257c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1816"/><div sID="gen2429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1816"/><hi type="bold">3. this shall be the priest's due from the people--</hi>All who offered sacrifices of thanksgiving or peace offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.31-Lev.7.33">Le 7:31-33</reference>) were ordered to give the breast and shoulder as perquisites to the priests. Here "the two cheeks" or head and "the maw" or stomach, deemed anciently a great dainty, are specified. But whether this is a new injunction, or a repetition of the old with the supplement of more details, it is not easy to determine. <div eID="gen2429" type="x-p"/>
entries.75bc18bcf4129f2d8fff1abc44c3ec5684e97086: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1817"/><div sID="gen2430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1817"/><hi type="bold">6-8. if a Levite ... come with all the desire of his mind--</hi>It appears that the Levites served in rotation from the earliest times; but, from their great numbers, it was only at infrequent intervals they could be called into actual service. Should any Levite, however, under the influence of eminent piety, resolve to devote himself wholly and continually to the sacred duties of the sanctuary, he was allowed to realize his ardent wishes; and as he was admitted to a share of the work, so also to a share of the remuneration. Though he might have private property, that was to form no ground for withholding or even diminishing his claim to maintenance like the other ministering priests. The reason or principle of the enactment is obvious (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13">1Co 9:13</reference>). At the same time, while every facility was afforded for the admission of such a zealous and self-denying officer, this admission was to be in an orderly manner: he was to minister "as all his brethren"--that is, a Gershonite with Gershonites; a Merarite with Merarites; so that there might be no derangement of the established courses. <div eID="gen2430" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb98398597946f607b6a0ac428fd55ee116ffbd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1818"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.18.9-Deut.18.14">De 18:9-14</reference>. The Abominations of the Nations Are to Be Avoided.</title> <div sID="gen2431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1818"/><hi type="bold">9-14. thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Le 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Le 19:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Le 19:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.4">Le 20:4</reference>). In spite of this express command, the people of Canaan, especially the Philistines, were a constant snare and stumbling block to the Israelites, on account of their divinations and superstitious practices. <div eID="gen2431" type="x-p"/>
entries.58ff8eed035d67fc69be0e70a4ead9d655ec4b10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1819"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.18.15-Deut.18.19">De 18:15-19</reference>. Christ the Prophet Is to Be Heard.</title> <div sID="gen2432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1819"/><hi type="bold">15-19. The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a prophet--</hi>The insertion of this promise, in connection with the preceding prohibition, might warrant the application (which some make of it) to that order of true prophets whom God commissioned in unbroken succession to instruct, to direct, and warn His people; and in this view the purport of it is, "There is no need to consult with diviners and soothsayers, as I shall afford you the benefit of divinely appointed prophets, for judging of whose credentials a sure criterion is given" (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.20-Deut.18.22">De 18:20-22</reference>). But the prophet here promised was pre-eminently the Messiah, for He alone was "like unto Moses" (see on <reference osisRef="Deut.34.10">De 34:10</reference>) "in His mediatorial character; in the peculiar excellence of His ministry; in the number, variety, and magnitude of His miracles; in His close and familiar communion with God; and in His being the author of a new dispensation of religion." This prediction was fulfilled fifteen hundred years afterwards and was expressly applied to Jesus Christ by Peter (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.22">Ac 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.23">23</reference>), and by Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.37">Ac 7:37</reference>). <div eID="gen2432" type="x-p"/>

entries.e5b81b71465bd1749aa2a1243b3d46e44cee3c00: <div eID="gen6781" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6782" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6783" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6783" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6782" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6784" type="x-p"/> The priests and Levites to have no inheritance, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.1">Deu 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.2">Deu 18:2</reference>. What is the priest's due, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.3-Deu.18.5">Deu 18:3-5</reference>. Of the Levites that come from any of the other cities, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.6-Deu.18.8">Deu 18:6-8</reference>. The Israelites must not copy the abominations of the former inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.9">Deu 18:9</reference>. None to cause his son or daughter to pass through the fire, or use any kind of divination or enchantment, as the former inhabitants did, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.10-Deu.18.14">Deu 18:10-14</reference>. The great prophet which God promised to raise up, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.15-Deu.18.19">Deu 18:15-19</reference>. Of false prophets, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.20">Deu 18:20</reference>; and how to discern them, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.21">Deu 18:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.22">Deu 18:22</reference>. <div eID="gen6784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6785" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6786" type="x-p"/> The priests the Levites - shall have no part - That is, says Rab. Maimon, they shall have no part in the spoils taken from an enemy.
entries.6b349de4f5c41726f1f035892ee181a91e0c88a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6787" type="x-p"/> The Lord is their inheritance - He is the portion of their souls; and as to their bodies, they shall live by the offerings of the Lord made by fire, i. e., the meat-offering, the sin-offering, and the trespass-offering; and whatever was the Lord's right, in these or other offerings, he gave to the priests.
entries.7101563aa28ae0d0d64dd4c7251182c8314fa00b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> Offer a sacrifice - זבחי הזבח zobechey hazzebach. The word זבח zebach is used to signify, not only an animal sacrificed to the Lord, but also one killed for common use. See <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1">Gen 46:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.17.1">Pro 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>. And in this latter sense it probably should be understood here; and, consequently, the command in this verse relates to what the people were to allow the priests and Levites from the animals slain for common use. The parts to be given to the priests were, <div eID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6789" type="x-p"/> 1. The shoulder, probably cut off from the beast with the skin on; so Maimonides. <div eID="gen6789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> 2. The two cheeks, which may include the whole head. <div eID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> 3. The maw - the whole of those intestines which are commonly used for food.
entries.999f693dc29664ac14fd27005545e22bd06ed86a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> The first-fruit also of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, etc. - All these firstfruits and firstlings were the Lord's portion, and these he gave to the priests.
entries.25f91764e9ff404f9287cae6190e587f8742541e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> The sale of his patrimony - So we find that, though the Levites might have no part of the land by lot, yet they were permitted to make purchases of houses, goods, and cattle, yea, of fields also. See the case of Abiathar, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.26">1Kgs 2:26</reference> (note), and of Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.7-Jer.32.8">Jer 32:7-8</reference> (note).
entries.84d65f1f2b20077d0bd2e41a034053a6aa5bd3af: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> To pass through the fire - Probably in the way of consecration to Molech, or some other deity. It is not likely that their being burnt to death is here intended. See on <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6795" type="x-p"/> Divination - קסם קסמים kosem kesamim, one who endeavors to find out futurity by auguries, using lots, etc. <div eID="gen6795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6796" type="x-p"/> Observer of times - מעונן meonen, one who pretends to foretell future events by present occurrences, and who predicts great political or physical changes from the aspects of the planets, eclipses, motion of the clouds, etc., etc. See on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.8">Gen 41:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6797" type="x-p"/> Enchanter - מנחש menachesh, from נחש nichesh, to view attentively; one who inspected the entrails of beasts, observed the flight of birds, etc., etc., and drew auguries thence. Some think divination by serpents is meant, which was common among the heathen. <div eID="gen6797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6798" type="x-p"/> A witch - מחשף mechashsheph, probably those who by means of drugs, herbs, perfumes, etc., pretended to bring certain celestial influences to their aid. See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Lev 19:26</reference>.
entries.1780d82d698126d67971083c2083708413a8b5a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6799" type="x-p"/> A charmer - חבר חבר chober chaber, one who uses spells; a peculiar conjunction, as the term implies, of words, or things, tying knots, etc., for the purposes of divination. This was a custom among the heathen, as we learn from the following verses: - <div eID="gen6799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6800" type="x-p"/> Necte Tribus Nodis ternos, Amarylli, colores: <div eID="gen6800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6801" type="x-p"/> Necte, Amarylli, modo; et Veneris, dic, vincula necto. <div eID="gen6801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6802" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. viii., ver. 77. "Knit with three Knots the fillets, knit them straight; <div eID="gen6802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6803" type="x-p"/> Then say, these Knots to love I consecrate." <div eID="gen6803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6804" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen6804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> A consulter with familiar spirits - שאל אוב shoel ob, a Pythoness, one who inquires by the means of one spirit to get oracular answers from another of a superior order. See on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> A wizard - ידעני yiddeoni, a wise one, a knowing one. Wizard was formerly considered as the masculine of witch, both practising divination by similar means. See on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.13">Exo 22:13</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6807" type="x-p"/> Or a necromancer - דרש אל המתים doresh el hammethim, one who seeks from or inquires of the dead. Such as the witch at Endor, who professed to evoke the dead, in order to get them to disclose the secrets of the spiritual world.
entries.1c288b42ba8ac48ed1da56b967a6b2df195f2783: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen6807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6808" type="x-p"/> The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet - Instead of diviners, observers of times, etc., God here promises to give them an infallible guide, who should tell them all things that make for their peace, so that his declarations should completely answer the end of all the knowledge that was pretended to be gained by the persons already specified. <div eID="gen6808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6809" type="x-p"/> Like unto me - Viz., a prophet, a legislator, a king, a mediator, and the head or chief of the people of God. This was the very person of whom Moses was the type, and who should accomplish all the great purposes of the Divine Being. Such a prophet as had never before appeared, and who should have no equal till the consummation of the world. <div eID="gen6809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6810" type="x-p"/> This prophet is the Lord Jesus, who was in the bosom of the Father, and who came to declare him to mankind. Every word spoken by him is a living infallible oracle from God himself; and must be received and obeyed as such, on pain of the eternal displeasure of the Almighty. See <reference osisRef="Deu.18.19">Deu 18:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Act.3.22">Act 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.3.23">Act 3:23</reference>; and see the conclusion of this chapter, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.22">Deu 18:22</reference> (note).
entries.a4c160137a915034f323b6ced331be5b061af2c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen6810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6811" type="x-p"/> If the thing follow not - It is worthy of remark that the prophets in general predicted those things which were shortly to come to pass, that the people might have the fullest proof of their Divine mission, and of the existence of God's providence in the administration of the affairs of men. <div eID="gen6811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6812" type="x-p"/> The promise contained in the <reference osisRef="Deu.18.15">Deu 18:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deu.18.18">Deu 18:18</reference> verses of this chapter has long been considered of the first importance in the controversies between the Christians and Jews. "Christ," says Ainsworth, "was to be a man, and of the stock of the Jews, by promise, because the people could not endure to hear the voice of God, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.16">Deu 18:16</reference>. And as in respect of his prophecy, so of the priesthood: for every high priest is taken from among men, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.1">Heb 5:1</reference>; and also of his kingdom, as in <reference osisRef="Deu.17.15">Deu 17:15</reference> : From among thy brethren shalt thou set a king over thee like unto me. "1. Christ alone was like unto Moses as a Prophet; for it is written, There arose not a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders which the Lord sent him to do, <reference osisRef="Deu.34.10">Deu 34:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.34.11">Deu 34:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.34.12">Deu 34:12</reference>. This therefore cannot be understood of the ordinary prophets which were raised up in Israel, but of Christ only, as the apostles expound it <reference osisRef="Act.2.22-Act.2.26">Act 2:22-26</reference>. <div eID="gen6812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6813" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ was like unto Moses in respect to his office of mediation between God and his people, <reference osisRef="Deu.5.5">Deu 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Tim 2:5</reference>; but greater than Moses as being the mediator of a better covenant, (or testament), which was established upon better promises, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.6">Heb 8:6</reference>. <div eID="gen6813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6814" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ was like unto Moses in excellency; for as Moses excelled all the prophets in speaking to God mouth to mouth, <reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Num 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.12.7">Num 12:7</reference>,<reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Num 12:8</reference>, so Christ excelled him and all men in that being in the bosom of the Father, he hath come down from heaven and declared God unto us, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>. <div eID="gen6814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6815" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ was like to Moses in faithfulness, but therein also excelling; for Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant, but Christ as the son over his own house, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">Heb 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5">Heb 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">Heb 3:6</reference>. <div eID="gen6815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6816" type="x-p"/> 5. Christ was like to Moses in signs and wonders, wherein he also excelled Moses, as the history of the Gospel shows; for he was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.19">Luk 24:19</reference>. A man approved of God among them, by miracles, signs, and wonders, which God did by him in the midst of them, <reference osisRef="Act.2.22">Act 2:22</reference>. For he did among them the works which no other man did, <reference osisRef="Joh.15.24">Joh 15:24</reference>. Unto him, that is, not unto the diviners, wizards, or any such like, but unto him, and him only; as Him thou shalt serve, <reference osisRef="Deu.6.13">Deu 6:13</reference>, is expounded, Him only, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.10">Mat 4:10</reference>. And though this is principally meant of Christ in person, of whom God said, Hear him, <reference osisRef="Mat.17.5">Mat 17:5</reference>; yet it implies also his ministers, as himself said, He that heareth you heareth me, <reference osisRef="Luk.10.16">Luk 10:16</reference>." To these may be added, <div eID="gen6816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6817" type="x-p"/> 6. As Moses was king among his people, in this respect Christ is like to him, but infinitely greater; for he is King of kings and Lord of lords, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.16">Rev 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Tim 6:15</reference>. <div eID="gen6817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6818" type="x-p"/> 7. He was like to Moses as a legislator. Moses gave laws to Israel by the authority and commandment of God, which the Jews have ever acknowledged as coming from the immediate inspiration of the Almighty: these are contained in the Pentateuch. Christ gave a new law, the Gospel contained in the four Evangelists and Acts of the Apostles, on which the Christian Church is founded, and by which all genuine Christians are governed both in heart and life. To all which may be added, <div eID="gen6818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6819" type="x-p"/> 8. That God never commissioned any human beings to give laws to mankind but Moses and Christ; and therefore, as a lawgiver, Christ alone resembles Moses; for to the present hour none but themselves have given laws in the name of God, which he has ratified and confirmed by the most indubitable and infallible signs, proofs, and miracles. <div eID="gen6819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6820" type="x-p"/> Dr. Jortin, in his Remarks on Ecclesiastical History, has drawn a parallel between Moses and Christ in a great number of particulars, which he concludes thus: "Let us search all the records of universal history, and see if we can find a man who was so like to Moses as Christ was, and so like to Christ as Moses was. If we cannot find such a one, then have we found Him of whom Moses in the law and the prophets did write to be Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God." On this subject see Ainsworth, Calmet, and Dodd, who have all marked this striking correspondence between Moses and Christ.  <chapter eID="Deut.18"/> <div eID="gen6820" type="x-p"/>

entries.111a0456ad1007fff6f1ffb1d77a0d91a9d92e37: <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1-Deut.18.2">Deu 18:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen2362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2363" type="x-p"/> The Rights of the Priests and Levites. - With reference to these, Moses repeats verbatim from Num 18:20, Num 18:23-24, the essential part of the rule laid down in Num 18: “<hi type="italic">The priests the Levites, the whole tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel</hi>.” “All the tribe of Levi” includes the priests and Levites. They were to eat the “firings of Jehovah and His inheritance,” as described in detail in Num 18. The inheritance of Jehovah consisted of the holy gifts as well as the sacrifices, i.e., the tithes, firstlings, and first-fruits. Moses felt it to be superfluous to enumerate these gifts one by one from the previous laws, and also to describe the mode of their application, or define how much belonged to the priests and how much to the Levites. However true it may be that the author assigns all these gifts to the Levites generally, the conclusion drawn from this, viz., that he was not acquainted with any distinction between priests and Levites, but placed the Levites entirely on a par with the priests, is quite a false one. For, apart from the evident distinction between the priests and Levites in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">Deu 18:1</reference>, where there would be no meaning in the clause, “all the tribe of Levi,” if the Levites were identical with the priests, the distinction is recognised and asserted as clearly as possible in what follows, when a portion of the slain-offerings is allotted to the priests in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.3-Deut.18.5">Deu 18:3-5</reference>, whilst in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.6-Deut.18.8">Deu 18:6-8</reference> the Levite is allowed to join in eating the altar gifts, if he come to the place of the sanctuary and perform service there. The repetition in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.2">Deu 18:2</reference> is an emphatic confirmation: “<hi type="italic">As He hath said unto them:</hi>” as in Deu 10:9.
entries.6afbebca5d7a573b6e6ea1fcc914845e6242408d: <reference osisRef="Deut.18.3-Deut.18.5">Deu 18:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen2363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2364" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">This shall be the right of the priests on the part of the people, on the part of those who slaughter slain-offerings, whether ox or sheep; he</hi> (the offerer) <hi type="italic">shall give the priest the shoulder, the cheek, and the stomach</hi>.” הזּרע, the shoulder, i.e., the front leg; see Num 6:19. הקּבה, the rough stomach, τὸ ἤνιστρον (lxx), i.e., the fourth stomach of ruminant animals, in which the digestion of the food is completed; Lat. <hi type="italic">omasus</hi> or <hi type="italic">abomasus</hi>, though the Vulgate has <hi type="italic">ventriculus</hi> here. On the choice of these three pieces in particular, <hi type="italic">Münster</hi> and <hi type="italic">Fagius</hi> observe that “the sheep possesses three principal parts, the head, the feet, and the trunk; and of each of these some portion was to be given to the priest who officiated” “Of each of these three principal parts of the animal,” says <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, “some valuable piece was to be presented: the shoulder at least, and the stomach, which was regarded as particularly fat, are seen at once to have been especially good.” That this arrangement is not at variance with the command in Lev 7:32., to give the wave-breast and heave-leg of the peace-offerings to the Lord for the priests, but simply enjoins a further gift to the priests on the part of the people, in addition to those portions which were to be given to the Lord for His servants, is sufficiently evident from the context, since the heave-leg and wave-breast belonged to the firings of Jehovah mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">Deu 18:1</reference>, which the priests had received as an inheritance from the Lord, that is to say, to the <hi type="italic">tenuphoth</hi> of the children of Israel, which the priests might eat with their sons and daughters, though only with such members of their house as were levitically clean (Num 18:11); and also from the words of the present command, viz., that the portions mentioned were to be a right of the priests <hi type="italic">on the part of the people</hi>, on the part of those who slaughtered slain-offerings, i.e., to be paid to the priest as a right that was due to him on the part of the people. משׁפּט was what the priest could justly claim. This right was probably accorded to the priests as a compensation for the falling off which would take place in their incomes in consequence of the repeal of the law that every animal was to be slaughtered at the sanctuary as a sacrifice (Lev 17; ; vid., Deu 12:15.). <div eID="gen2364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2365" type="x-p"/> The only thing that admits of dispute is, whether this gift was to be presented from every animal that was slaughtered at home for private use, or only from those which were slaughtered for sacrificial meals, and therefore at the place of the sanctuary. Against the former view, for which appeal is made to <hi type="italic">Philo, Josephus</hi> (Ant. iv. 4, 4), and the Talmud, we may adduce not only “the difficulty of carrying out such a plan” (was every Israelite who slaughtered an ox, a sheep, or a goat to carry the pieces mentioned to the priests’ town, which might be many miles away, or were the priests to appoint persons to collect them?), but the general use of the words זבח זבח. The noun זבח always signifies either slaughtering for a sacrificial meal or a slain sacrifice, and the verb זבח is never applied to ordinary slaughtering (for which שׁחט is the verb used), except in <reference osisRef="Deut.12.15">Deu 12:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.12.21">Deu 12:21</reference> in connection with the repeal of the law that every slaughtering was to be a שׁלמים זבח (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.5">Lev 17:5</reference>); and there the use of the word זבח, instead of שׁחט, may be accounted for from the allusion to this particular law. At the same time, the Jewish tradition is probably right, when it understands by the הזּבח זבחי in this verse, κατ' ïé̓͂êïí èṍåéí åõ̓ù÷é́áò å̔́íåêá (<hi type="italic">Josephus</hi>), or ἔξω τοῦ βωμοῦ θυομένοις ἕνεκα κρεωφαγίας (<hi type="italic">Philo</hi>), or, as in the <hi type="italic">Mishnah Chol.</hi> (x. 1), refers the gift prescribed in this passage to the חולין, <hi type="italic">profana</hi>, and not to the מוקדשׁרן, <hi type="italic">consecrata</hi>, that is to say, places it in the same category with the first-fruits, the tithe of tithes, and other less holy gifts, which might be consumed outside the court of the temple and the holy city (compare <hi type="italic">Reland</hi>, <hi type="italic">Antiqq</hi>. ss. P. ii. c. 4, §11, with P. ii. c. 8, §10). In all probability, the reference is to the slaughtering of oxen, sheep, or goats which were not intended for <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> in the more limited sense, i.e., for one of the three species of peace-offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.15-Lev.7.16">Lev 7:15-16</reference>), but for festal meals in the broader sense, which were held in connection with the sacrificial meals prepared from the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi>. For it is evident that the meals held by the people at the annual feasts when they had to appear before the Lord were not all <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> meals, but that other festal meals were held in connection with these, in which the priests and Levites were to share, from the laws laid down with reference to the so-called second tithe, which could not only be turned into money by those who lived at a great distance from the sanctuary, such money to be applied to the purchase of the things required for the sacrificial meals at the place of the sanctuary, but which might also be appropriated every third year to the preparation of love-feasts for the poor in the different towns of the land (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.22-Deut.14.29">Deu 14:22-29</reference>). For in this case the animals were not slaughtered or sacrificed as <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi>, at all events not in the latter instance, because the slaughtering did not take place at the sanctuary. If therefore we restrict the gift prescribed here to the slaughtering of oxen and sheep or goats for such sacrificial meals in the wider sense, not only are the difficulties connected with the execution of this command removed, but also the objection, which arises out of the general use of the expression זבח זבח, to the application of this expression to every slaughtering that took place for domestic use. And beside this, the passage in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13-1Sam.2.16">1Sa 2:13-16</reference>, to which <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> calls attention, furnishes a historical proof that the priests could claim a portion of the flesh of the slain-offerings in addition to the heave-leg and wave-breast, since it is there charged as a sin on the part of the sons of Eli, not only that they took out of the cauldrons as much of the flesh which was boiling as they could take up with three-pronged forks, but that before the fat was burned upon the altar they asked for the pieces which belonged to the priest, to be given to them not cooked, but raw. From this <hi type="italic">Michaelis</hi> has drawn the correct conclusion, that even at that time the priests had a right to claim that, in addition to the portions of the sacrifices appointed by Moses in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.34">Lev 7:34</reference>, a further portion of the thank-offerings should be given to them; though he does not regard the passage as referring to the law before us, since he supposes this to relate to every slaughtered animal which was not placed upon the altar.
entries.da3ba78c5e5ce2b553c8042de68d040658dfff74: <reference osisRef="Deut.18.6">Deu 18:6</reference> <div eID="gen2367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2368" type="x-p"/> As the priests were to be remembered for their service on the part of the people (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.3-Deut.18.5">Deu 18:3-5</reference>), so the Levite also, who came from one of the towns of the land with all the desire of his soul to the place of the sanctuary, to minister there in the name of the Lord, was to eat a similar portion to all his Levitical brethren who stood there in service before the Lord. The verb גּוּר (sojourned) does not presuppose that the Levites were houseless, but simply that they had no hereditary possession in the land as the other tribes had, and merely lived like sojourners among the Israelites in the towns which were given up to them by the other tribes (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.12.12">Deu 12:12</reference>). “<hi type="italic">All his brethren the Levites</hi>” are the priests and those Levites who officiated at the sanctuary as assistants to the priests. It is assumed, therefore, that only a part of the Levites were engaged at the sanctuary, and the others lived in their towns. The apodosis follows in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.8">Deu 18:8</reference>, “<hi type="italic">part like part shall they eat</hi>,” sc., the new-comer and those already there. The former was to have the same share to eat as the latter, and to be maintained from the revenues of the sanctuary. These revenues are supposed to be already apportioned by the previous laws, so that they by no means abolish the distinction between priests and Levites. We are not to think of those portions of the sacrifices and first-fruits only which fell to the lot of the priests, nor of the tithe alone, or of the property which flowed into the sanctuary through vows or free-will offerings, or in any other way, and was kept in the treasury and storehouse, but of tithes, sacrificial portions, and free-will offerings generally, which were not set apart exclusively for the priests. וגו ממכּריו לבד, “<hi type="italic">beside his sold with the fathers</hi>,” i.e., independently of what he receives from the sale of his patrimony. ממכּר, the sale, then the thing sold, and the price or produce of what is sold, like מכר in Num 20:19. לבד is unusual without מן, and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> would read ממּכריו, from מכריו and מן, in consequence. האבות על stands for בּית־אבות על (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.6.25">Exo 6:25</reference>; κατὰ τὴν πατρίαν, lxx), according to or with the fathers’ houses, i.e., the produce of the property which he possesses according to his family descent, or which is with his kindred. Whether על in this passage signifies “according to the measure of,” or “with,” in the sense of keeping or administering, cannot be decided. As the law in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.33-Lev.25.34">Lev 25:33-34</reference>, simply forbids the sale of the pasture grounds belonging to the Levites, but permits the sale of their houses, a Levite who went to the sanctuary might either let his property in the Levitical town, and draw the yearly rent, or sell the house which belonged to him there. In any case, these words furnish a convincing proof that there is no foundation for the assertion that the book of Deuteronomy assumes or affirms that the Levites were absolutely without possessions.
entries.90f865a036c02aa16289f16548763f587320e9d0: <reference osisRef="Deut.18.9-Deut.18.22">Deu 18:9-22</reference> <div eID="gen2368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2369" type="x-p"/> The Gift of Prophecy. - The Levitical priests, as the stated guardians and promoters of the law, had to conduct all the affairs of Israel with the Lord, not only instructing the people out of the law concerning the will of God, but sustaining and promoting the living fellowship with the Lord both of individuals and of the whole congregation, by the offering of sacrifices and service at the altar. But if the covenant fellowship with Himself and His grace, in which Jehovah had placed Israel as His people of possession, was to be manifested and preserved as a living reality amidst all changes in the political development of the nation and in the circumstances of private life, it would not do for the revelations from God to cease with the giving of the law and the death of Moses. For, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> observes, “however the revelation of the law might aim at completeness, and even have regard to the more remote circumstances of the future, as, for example, where the king is referred to; yet in the transition from extraordinary circumstances into a more settled condition, which it foretells in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.14">Deu 17:14</reference>, and which actually took place under Samuel when the nation grew older (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.25">Deu 4:25</reference>), and in the decline and apostasy which certainly awaited it according to <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16-Deut.31.29">Deu 31:16-29</reference>, when false prophets should arise, by whom they were in danger of being led astray (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.2">Deu 13:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">Deu 18:20</reference>), as well as in the restoration which would follow after the infliction of punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.29-Deut.4.30">Deu 4:29-30</reference>; Deu 30:1.); in all these great changes which awaited Israel from inward necessity, the revelation of the will of the Lord which they possessed in the law would nevertheless be insufficient.” The priesthood, with its ordinances, would not suffice for that. As the promise of direct communications from God through the Urim and Thummim of the high priest was restricted to the single circumstance of the right of the whole congregation being endangered, and did not extend to the satisfaction of the religious necessities of individuals, it could afford no godly satisfaction to that desire for supernatural knowledge which arose at times in the hearts of individuals, and for which the heathen oracles made such ample provision in ungodly ways. If Israel therefore was to be preserved in faithfulness towards God, and attain the end of its calling as the congregation of the Lord, it was necessary that the Lord should make known His counsel and will at the proper time through the medium of prophets, and bestow upon it in sure prophetic words what the heathen nations endeavoured to discover and secure by means of augury and soothsaying. This is the point of view from which Moses promises the sending of prophets in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15-Deut.18.18">Deu 18:15-18</reference>, and lays down in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.19-Deut.18.22">Deu 18:19-22</reference> the criteria for distinguishing between true and false prophets, as we may clearly see from the fact that in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.9-Deut.18.14">Deu 18:9-14</reference> he introduces this promise with a warning against resorting to heathen augury, soothsaying, and witchcraft.  <reference osisRef="Deut.18.9-Deut.18.11">Deu 18:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen2369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2370" type="x-p"/> When Israel came into the land of Canaan, it was “<hi type="italic">not to learn to do like the abominations of these nations</hi>” (the Canaanites or heathen). There was not to be found in it any who caused his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, i.e., any worshipper of Moloch (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference>), or one who practised soothsaying (see at Num 23:23), or a wizard (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Lev 19:26</reference>), or a snake-charmer (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Lev 19:26</reference>), or a conjurer, or one who pronounced a ban (חבר חבר, probably referring to the custom of binding or banning by magical knots), a necromancer and wise man (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>), or one who asked the dead, i.e., who sought oracles from the dead. Moses groups together all the words which the language contained for the different modes of exploring the future and discovering the will of God, for the purpose of forbidding every description of soothsaying, and places the prohibition of Moloch-worship at the head, to show the inward connection between soothsaying and idolatry, possibly because februation, or passing children through the fire in the worship of Moloch, was more intimately connected with soothsaying and magic than and other description of idolatry.

entries.92256af9093fcf7fe4b94b2569cc3e065b0fac73: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.18.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.18.1" sID="gen12470" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">The priests, the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi.</hi> This chapter contains three principal heads; for <hi type="italic">first, </hi>God shews that there was no reason why the Israelites should be aggrieved at paying tithes to the Levites, and at remitting the first-fruits and other oblations to the priests, since this tribe was deprived of their inheritance. <hi type="italic">Secondly, </hi>He obviates all quarrels, and prevents unlawful gains and pilferings, by assigning their just share to the priests and Levites. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, </hi>He defines how the oblations should be parted among them, and what part of the victims the priests were to take. As to the first clause, since God was as it were the lot of their inheritance, they justly claimed to themselves the right which he had transferred to them. If it were disagreeable to the people that their revenue should be tithed, God came as it were between, and declaring that it was His property in His right as King, appointed the Levites to be His stewards and collectors for receiving it. There was then no ground for any one to raise a dispute, unless he chose professedly to rob God. But this declaration often occurs; since it was of great importance that the people should be assured that God accounted as received by Himself what He had assigned to the Levites; not. only lest any portion should be withheld from them, but also that every one should willingly pay the lawful dues of God’s ministers; and again, lest any should wickedly murmur because the first-fruits and some portion of the sacrifices were appropriated for the subsistence of the priests. Another reason is also expressed, why the honor assigned to the priests should be paid without grudging; viz., because God had appointed them to be the ministers of His service; but “the laborer is worthy of his hire."<div eID="gen12471" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.18.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12470" osisID="Deut.18.1" type="section"/>
entries.a1f5423267632be47e48086bfa55fd052e11dea2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.18.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.18.3" sID="gen12472" type="section"/> <div sID="gen12473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">And this shall be the priests’ due.</hi> It is not only for the sake of the priests that God enumerates what He would have them receive, that they may obtain what is their own without murmuring or dispute; but He also has regard to the people,<hi type="italic"> </hi>lest the priests should basely and greedily take more than their due; which sacred history relates to have been done by the sons of Eli, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.23">1 Samuel 2:23</reference>,) for they had advanced to such a degree of licentiousness, that, like robbers, they seized violently on whatever their lust desired. Lest therefore they should give way to this gross covetousness, God prescribes to them certain limits, to which they were to confine themselves, so that if they transgressed them, it was easy for any of the people to convict them of avarice.<div eID="gen12473" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.18.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen12472" osisID="Deut.18.3" type="section"/>

6. And if a Levite come. This third head more clearly explains what is elsewhere more obscurely declared; for God seemed to curtail from the Levites whatever He gave to the priests. But He now more distinctly places the priests in the first rank, yet so that they should admit the Levites on the score of their labor’s to a share of the oblations. This is the sum of the law, that the Levites who remained at home, should be content with the tithes, and touch nothing of the other offerings; but that from whithersoever they should come to the sanctuary, they were to be accounted as ministers and take their proper place. By this law then, it was provided that none should be excluded on the ground of the intermission of their duties; and that the condition of those that dwelt elsewhere should not be worse than of those who lived at Jerusalem. For although they might reside in other cities, they did not altogether cease from their ministry, since they had other duties to perform besides that of sacrificing the victims. Yet those who entirely devoted themselves to the work of the sanctuary, were endowed by God with double honor; since it was by no means just that they should be defrauded of their maintenance, who bade adieu to domestic cares and labors, and occupied themselves totally in holy offices.
